correctness.rationale: The condition \(k-s_i\ge\min\{c_i,3\}\) is necessary: one omission in a part needs an outside selected vertex for domination, two omitted attacked vertices force two distinct outside defenders, and if at least three vertices remain omitted then a third outside selected vertex must survive the two-defender move. It is sufficient by splitting attacks into the same-part and distinct-part cases; in the latter, the two closed-neighborhood candidate sets cover all of \(S\), so with \(|S|\ge2\) they admit distinct representatives, and the replacement meets both attacked parts. The coefficient formulas count exactly the heavy-part violations; two bad-part events can overlap only for \(k=4\), producing the stated correction. An independent definition-level brute-force replay on representative profiles through order eight found no disagreement with the criterion.
risks: The definition uses distinct attacked vertices and distinct defenders, matching the 2020 primary source; differently named secure 2-domination is a separate invariant.

value.rationale: Two-secure domination models simultaneous attacks and is algorithmically difficult in broad graph classes. On a canonical dense family, the three-guard cap collapses the feasibility problem to part occupancies and yields all cardinality coefficients, a structurally useful exact classification rather than a routine minimum-value calculation.
risks: The theorem is family-specific and does not transfer automatically to graphs whose non-neighborhoods are not parts.
